summary: Describes situations where the Babel routing protocol has proven useful and where it arguably fits better than more mature protocols. Babel is a distance-vector protocol with mechanisms for loop avoidance and starvation avoidance, and this document surveys its niches.

plainLanguage.summary: Babel is a way for routers to share directions. This lists the places where it works especially well compared to older options.

questions: when to use the babel routing protocol
how does babel avoid routing loops
subtitle: When a simple distance-vector routing protocol works better than complex alternatives

tldr.problem: Traditional routing protocols like OSPF and IS-IS are complex and assume stable, well-managed networks. Some deployment scenarios need a simpler approach that handles unusual topologies and metrics.
tldr.mechanism: Babel is a distance-vector protocol based on distributed Bellman-Ford with loop avoidance (feasibility) and recovery mechanisms (sequenced routes) that do not require reliable transport or network stability.
tldr.outcome: Babel has found successful deployment niches in heterogeneous networks, large-scale overlays, mesh networks, and small unmanaged networks where its simplicity and robustness outweigh the overheads of more complex protocols.

today: RFC 8965 is an Informational RFC that describes where Babel routing has proven useful. The RFC does not define the Babel protocol itself (that is RFC 8966); it surveys the deployment scenarios and niches where Babel works well compared to more mature protocols.

sections.title: What is Babel
sections.content:
Babel is a distance-vector routing protocol designed to fill niches where traditional protocols like OSPF and IS-IS do not fit well. The protocol is based on the distributed Bellman-Ford algorithm, a familiar and simple concept that routers have used since RIP; however, Babel adds two important mechanisms to make it practical in real deployments: feasibility, which avoids routing loops, and sequenced routes, which recover from edge cases where feasibility creates starvation (where a router temporarily has no route to a destination even though one exists).

Because Babel does not assume reliable transport, ordered delivery, or transitive links, it can work in network environments that would confuse protocols designed for traditional Internet backbones. This flexibility makes it useful in several practical scenarios.
sections.plainLanguage: Babel is a routing protocol that does not need perfect networks to work. It just tells routers: ask your neighbors what paths they know, pick the shortest one, and keep checking if things change.

sections.title: Properties and Limitations
sections.content:
Babel is conceptually simple: it consists of a familiar algorithm augmented with three well-defined mechanisms. This simplicity is its greatest strength. The protocol is easy to explain, and multiple independent, interoperable implementations exist; one was reportedly debugged in just two nights.

The protocol is also robust with respect to unusual networks. It works in networks with non-transitive links, unstable link costs, and other properties that would challenge link-state protocols. Its weak requirements make it suitable for novel metrics such as continuous measurements or fluctuating measurements based on packet loss rates.

However, Babel has limitations. It relies on periodic updates to recover from certain pathologies, which makes it unsuitable for large, stable networks where an efficient reliable transport protocol would reduce control traffic, and for low-power networks where battery power is scarce. Additionally, Babel assumes that every router maintains a full routing table, making it unsuitable for memory-constrained devices that need to learn only a default route. Route aggregation recovery is slow in some cases when nodes are retracted.
sections.plainLanguage: Babel is simple to understand and works in messy networks, but it sends traffic regularly even when nothing changes. This uses power and bandwidth in networks that do not need it.

sections.title: The Algorithm in Practice
sections.content:
Babel uses feasibility, a mechanism pioneered by EIGRP, to avoid the pathological convergence problem in distance-vector protocols known as "counting to infinity". This mechanism works by rejecting any route that does not satisfy a feasibility condition based on the route's advertised distance and a router's own distance to the destination. Feasibility is conservative: it rejects some loop-free routes alongside looping routes.

When feasibility causes starvation (a router has no valid route when one actually exists), Babel uses sequenced routes and explicit requests to recover. Routers can announce a sequence number with routes; when a router detects starvation, it requests a higher sequence number. This triggers rapid propagation of a new route announcement and clears the starvation in time proportional to the network diameter.

Unlike link-state protocols, Babel does not flood updates reliably or assume ordered delivery. Routers can send triggered updates when topology changes, retractions when routes fail, and seqno requests to resolve starvation. The protocol works correctly even with packet loss and out-of-order delivery, making it robust in wireless and other imperfect networks.
sections.plainLanguage: When routing goes wrong and every router says a destination is unreachable (even though it is not), Babel has a trick: ask for a newer route announcement, and the network fixes itself quickly.

sections.title: Where Babel Works Well
sections.content:
Babel has been successfully deployed in four main types of networks. Heterogeneous networks combine wired backbones with wireless mesh edges; Babel handles both Internet-style prefix routing and flat mesh routing with variable link quality. Large-scale overlay networks span thousands of tunnels across continents; Babel can work with metrics computed from link latency and tolerates the unstable metrics that arise when latency changes rapidly.

In pure mesh networks, wireless routers use Babel as a competitive alternative to protocols like OLSR-ETX, though this niche is already well-served. Finally, small unmanaged networks such as home or small office networks can use Babel as a replacement for RIP, with the added benefit that it routes both IPv6 and IPv4 in a single protocol instance and handles wireless links well.

These deployments exploit Babel's simplicity, robustness to unusual topologies and metrics, and support for multiple address families in a single protocol. The RFC emphasizes that these are the niches where Babel fits better than more mature alternatives, not that these are the only networks where Babel could run.
sections.plainLanguage: Babel works well in home networks, mesh networks, and networks built from thousands of tunnels on the Internet. It works where you do not have perfect fiber connections or where routers are simple.

sections.title: Security and Extensions
sections.content:
As a distance-vector protocol, Babel trusts reachability information from its neighbors by default. If Babel runs over unprotected networks, routing traffic should be protected with cryptography. Two mechanisms have been defined: Babel-MAC is a simple mechanism that guarantees authenticity, integrity, and replay protection using symmetric keys, while Babel-DTLS is more complex but provides confidentiality and asymmetric key support.

The protocol's design emphasizes extensibility. Its packet format includes features that make it easy to add extensions, and the straightforward design principles make it possible to verify that new extensions do not violate the protocol's core assumptions. Deployed extensions include source-specific routing (SADR) for cheap multihoming and RTT-based routing for overlay networks. Other experimental extensions exist but have not yet seen wide deployment.

One privacy consideration: the routing information a mobile node announces can be sufficient to determine its physical location with reasonable precision, which may be a concern in some scenarios.
sections.plainLanguage: Babel routers trust each other by default, so bad routers can announce false routes. Use encryption to protect routing traffic. New features can be added to Babel without breaking it.
